title: Numbers, prices, and haggling at the bozor
goal: Count to a thousand, ask the price with *qancha*, use the counting ending *-ta*, and haggle without sounding rude.
bekal: say the numbers 1–100 and multiples of a thousand
haggle with *arzonroq boʻladimi?* — a phrase that will save you money every day

dialogs.title: Dialog — Chorsu bozorida
dialogs.intro: Budi is standing in front of a mountain of fruit. The seller, a middle-aged woman, has been watching him for a while.

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.id: Come on, young man! The fruit is really sweet!

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Assalomu alaykum, opa. Bu uzum qancha turadi?
lines.id: Hello, ma'am. How much are these grapes?
lines.literal: hello, older-sister. this grapes how-much stands?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Bir kilosi yigirma besh ming soʻm.
lines.literal: one kilo-its twenty five thousand som.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Oh, that's expensive! Can it be cheaper?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Mayli, sizga yigirma ming. Nechta kilo olasiz?
lines.id: All right, for you twenty thousand. How many kilos will you take?
lines.literal: all-right, you-to twenty thousand. how-many kilo take-you?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Ikki kilo, iltimos. Anor ham bormi?
lines.id: Two kilos, please. Do you have pomegranates too?
lines.literal: two kilo, please. pomegranate also there-is-?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Albatta. Anor donasi olti ming soʻm.
lines.id: Of course. Pomegranates are six thousand som each.
lines.literal: of-course. pomegranate piece-its six thousand som.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Uchta anor bering. Hammasi qancha boʻldi?
lines.id: Three pomegranates, please. How much is it all together?
lines.literal: three-items pomegranate give. all-of-it how-much became?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Qirq ming plus oʻn sakkiz ming — ellik sakkiz ming soʻm.
lines.id: Forty thousand plus eighteen thousand — fifty-eight thousand som.
lines.literal: forty thousand plus ten eight thousand — fifty eight thousand som.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Here, sixty thousand. Do you have change?

lines.speaker: Sotuvchi:
lines.text: Bor, ikki ming. Rahmat, yana keling!
lines.id: Yes, two thousand. Thank you, come again!
lines.literal: there-is, two thousand. thanks, again come!

notes: **Qancha turadi? literally "how much does it stand?".** The verb *turmoq* (to stand) is used for prices — just as English *cost* comes from Latin *constare*, "to stand firm". A shorter form that's just as correct: *Bu necha pul?* — "this how-much money?".

**-ku sticks on the end to show surprise.** *Qimmat-ku!* = "That's expensive!" It isn't a word, just seasoning; leaving it out is still correct, using it makes you sound like you've been around a while.
**Mayli = "all right".** One word to agree, give in, or close a deal. In Uzbekistan you'll hear it dozens of times a day, often doubled: *mayli-mayli*.
**Bir kilosi = "one kilo of it".** The ending *-si* here isn't about ownership but marks a portion: "the one kilo of it". Same pattern: *donasi* (per piece), *bittasi* (one of them).

**Big numbers have no "and".** *Ellik sakkiz ming* = 58,000, literally "fifty eight thousand". Uzbek money comes in big numbers — lunch can cost 40,000 som — so the numbers in this unit aren't school drills but everyday survival.

grammars.title: Numbers: ten basic words, the rest is assembly
body: Learn the first ten rows and the nine tens. Every other number is built from these, with no exceptions at all.
after: **The teens = *oʻn* + the unit**, written as separate words: *oʻn bir* (11), *oʻn besh* (15), *oʻn toʻqqiz* (19). The other tens work exactly the same: *yigirma uch* (23), *qirq yetti* (47), *toʻqson toʻqqiz* (99).

Above a hundred: *yuz* (100), *ikki yuz* (200), *ming* (1,000), *besh ming* (5,000), *million* (1,000,000). Note that **there's no "one"** in front of *yuz* and *ming* when the amount is just one: 100 = *yuz*, 1,000 = *ming*.

⚠️ Six numbers contain letters that are easy to mix up. *Toʻrt* uses *oʻ*; so do *oʻn* and *oʻttiz*. But *olti*, *oltmish*, and *nol* use plain *o*, which is pronounced **å**. Read this row out loud until you hear the difference: *oʻn — olti — oʻttiz — oltmish*.

grammars.title: -ta: the ending that appears when you count things
body: Many Asian languages put a counter word between the number and the noun — like English "three **pieces** of cake" or "two **head** of cattle", but for everything. Uzbek does the same, with one ending attached to the number.
after: ⚠️ **After a number, the noun stays singular.** *Uchta kitob*, not *uchta kitoblar*. The number already shows the amount.

*-ta* is used when things are **counted one by one**. For measures and amounts, the number stands bare: *ikki kilo uzum*, *uch soat*, *besh ming soʻm*. So *bitta non* (one loaf of bread) but *bir kilo non* (one kilo of bread).
For people there's a respectful form, *nafar*: *besh nafar talaba* (five students). It's used in official writing and announcements; on the street *beshta talaba* is enough.

blocks.text: Haggling in Uzbekistan isn't a fight but a friendly ritual both sides enjoy. Bargaining with a smile is seen as polite; paying the first price without asking actually seems strange.

blocks.text: One last-resort line if the price is truly outrageous: *Boshqa joyda arzonroq* — "it's cheaper somewhere else". Say it while taking half a step away, and see what happens.

sections.title: Fruit, bread, and the rest on the shelf

blocks.text: Uzbekistan is a land of fruit. Its melons and grapes have been famous since Silk Road times, and Uzbeks are truly proud of them — praising the fruit is the fastest way to win over the seller.

*Non* isn't just bread. It's round, stamped in the middle, and treated with respect: it must never be put upside down, never thrown away, and it's broken by hand — never cut with a knife. If you're a guest in an Uzbek home, breaking the *non* is the first part of eating together.

⚠️ *Anor* (pomegranate) and *shakar* (sugar) are Persian and Arabic words that traveled far: *shakar* is the same word as English *sugar* (via Arabic *sukkar*), and *anor* is Persian *anār*, also found in Hindi and Turkish (*nar*).
